title: HTML Tables
summary: Build data tables with thead, tbody, th and td, make them accessible with scope and caption, merge cells with colspan and rowspan, and know when not to use a table.
introduction: Tables present data that has rows and columns: prices, timetables, comparison charts. HTML tables have a reputation for being complicated because they were once abused for page layout. Used for actual data and structured with header cells and a caption, they are straightforward and work beautifully with screen readers. This lesson builds one up step by step.
learningObjectives: Structure a table with caption, thead, tbody, tr, th and td
Associate header cells with data cells using scope
Span cells across columns and rows

blocks.text: A `<table>` contains rows (`<tr>`); each row contains header cells (`<th>`) or data cells (`<td>`).
Browsers show tables without borders by default; the borders in these previews come from a little CSS. Styling tables is covered in the [CSS tutorial](/tutorials/css).

Group the header row in `<thead>`, the data in `<tbody>` and totals in `<tfoot>`. Add a `<caption>` as the first child to give the table a title that screen readers announce. The `scope` attribute on `<th>` states whether the header applies to its column or its row.

blocks.text: With `scope` in place, a screen reader reading the cell `285` announces "Groceries, February, 285", which is exactly what a sighted reader works out from the position.
`colspan` makes a cell span several columns; `rowspan` makes it span several rows. The merged cell replaces the cells it covers, so the following rows contain fewer cells.

blocks.text: Count your cells after adding `colspan` or `rowspan`. A row with too many cells pushes extra cells outside the grid, and a row with too few leaves gaps. Keep merged cells to a minimum; complex merges are hard for screen readers to describe.
When not to use a table

Tables are for tabular data only. Do not use them to position a sidebar next to content or to line up form fields; that is layout, which belongs to CSS grid and flexbox. A layout table confuses screen readers, which announce it as data, and makes responsive design nearly impossible.

blocks.title: Responsive tables
blocks.text: Wide tables overflow on phones. The usual fix is a wrapper element with `overflow-x: auto` in CSS so the table scrolls horizontally instead of breaking the page.

questions.question: Which attribute tells a screen reader that a header cell applies to its whole row?
questions.explanation: `scope="row"` associates the header with the cells in its row; `scope="col"` with its column.
